did_you_know.text: Did you know? Psalm 70 opens with the heading: “For the director of music. Of David. To bring to remembrance.” The heading presents the psalm as a psalm of David and uses the phrase “to bring to remembrance.”

Did you know? The psalmist makes two brief and urgent requests: “O God, save me,” and “LORD, hasten to help me.” This emphasizes both the request for deliverance and the plea for help to come quickly.

Did you know? The psalmist asks that those who seek his life and desire his harm be put to shame and disgrace, and even retreat. The request describes their downfall in terms of shame and withdrawal, not physical harm.

Did you know? The expression “because of their shame” describes the psalmist’s enemies retreating because of their disgrace. The verse also mentions their cry, “Aha! Aha!”—presented as part of their behavior toward the psalmist.

Did you know? Alongside the description of those who seek harm, the psalm sets apart another group: “all who seek you.” They are called to rejoice and be glad in God, and always to declare: “Let God be magnified.”

Did you know? At the end, the psalmist describes himself as “poor and needy,” again asks God to hasten to him, and declares: “You are my help and my deliverer.” The psalm ends with an explicit request: “Do not delay.”
